Well, doctor, that's... that's a sad thing to admit, really. Because if you asked anyone who knows me, they'd tell you I used to be quite the busy bee. My days were just full of things I loved doing. Like my painting... I used to look forward to my watercolors so much. And it’s the exact same story with my dance class. Oh, I used to love Tuesday mornings! A group of us would go down to the community center for line dancing. We'd dance to those old country songs, and I even bought these special shoes with suede on the bottoms so you can slide real nice on the wood floor without scuffing it up. But now... I haven't been in months. I just look at those shoes sitting in the bottom of the closet and think, what's the point? I can't muster up a single ounce of joy for the music anymore, let alone the dancing. 

Even just walking with the ladies... I used to do that every Thursday, rain or shine, unless it was pouring, of course. We’d do a whole big loop around the park, catching up on all the neighborhood news, seeing whose grandkids were doing what, looking at the gardens. I just don't care about the walk, or the chatting, or any of it. It's just like all the color has washed right out of everything.

Oh, doctor, the guilt... the guilt is just awful. It really eats me alive. I do feel bad about those nighttime thoughts, yes, because I know how much that would hurt my family, but... well, if I'm being completely honest with you, the thing that really brings on the worst of the guilt, the thing that just makes me sick to my stomach, is how I've been feeling about my aunt.

Well, my weight... you know, I haven't really stepped on the scale in a while. I used to keep it right there in the bathroom, tucked under the vanity, the one with the little blue dial that my husband bought me years ago. Sleep... oh, sleep has just been... well, it's just fine, really. I mean, I haven't noticed any real trouble with it. I go to bed around the same time I always do, usually right after the ten o'clock news finishes up. I like to watch the local broadcast, you know, just to see what the weather is going to do the next day, even though I hardly go out anymore. Anyway, after that, I make sure the front door is locked, check that the stove is off—I have to check it two or three times just to be absolutely sure, a habit I picked up from my mother—and then I head to bed. 

And once I'm in bed, I just... I sleep. I guess I must be sleeping alright because I don't remember tossing and turning or waking up and looking at the clock at all hours of the night. My husband used to do that, bless him. He'd wake up at two in the morning and go sit in the living room and read his history books. But me, I just pull the covers up, and the next thing I know, it's morning and I have to get up to start the oatmeal for my aunt. So, no, I wouldn't say I've had any trouble sleeping. It's just the usual routine, night in and night out, nothing out of the ordinary at all.

Well, now that you mention it... yes, I suppose I have been moving a bit differently. My husband, bless his heart, he actually brought it up just the other day. We were in the kitchen, and I was trying to get the good china down from the top shelf of the hutch—the set we got for our 25th anniversary, the one with the little gold rim—and he came in and told me that I move like everything takes extra effort now. I used to just zip in and out, you know? Grab my cart, go straight to the produce, pick out the firmest tomatoes, and be done with it. But lately, I'll go down to the Piggly Wiggly—I still go to the one on Elm Street because the produce manager, Mr. Henderson, always makes sure the apples are fresh—and I'll find myself just... standing there. I'll stand right in front of the display, looking at the fruit, and I just can't seem to make my hand reach out and pick up what I came for. It's like my brain knows what to do, but my body just takes so, so long to catch up. I just stand there for the longest time, staring, before I can finally get my arm to move and put a simple bag of carrots in the basket. It’s just so much harder to get anything done.

So yes, four whole months of this. Four months of going to sleep just hoping I wouldn't have to do it all over again the next day. It’s a long time to feel like that, isn't it? I kept waiting to just bounce back like I used to, thinking maybe once we got into a routine with her it would lift, but the days just keep blurring together and that dark cloud just stays right there.\n\nDoctor: Do you still find pleasure in activities that you used to enjoy before these feelings started?\n\nPatient: Well, doctor, that's... that's a sad thing to admit, really. I'd paint little birds, mostly, or whatever flowers were blooming out front in the beds. Appetite... well, no, I wouldn't say my appetite has changed much at all. I still eat my regular meals, just like always. It's funny you ask, though, because with how completely exhausted I feel, you'd think I just wouldn't have the stomach for it, but I still get hungry right on schedule. 

Like for breakfast... well, after I make that oatmeal for my aunt, I usually fix myself a slice of toast. Just one slice, usually the honey wheat, toasted right to a nice golden brown. I have this older toaster, a Sunbeam, the chrome kind—they just don't make them like that anymore, do they? It pops up perfect every single time. And I'll put a little butter on it, and maybe some of the strawberry preserves my neighbor, Mrs. Gable, brings over. She makes it from scratch every summer, boils the glass jars and seals them with the wax and everything. She's such a sweet lady, always checking in on me. 

And then for lunch, it's usually just a half a sandwich or a little bowl of soup. Campbell's tomato, mostly, especially when it's damp out. I'll heat it up on the stove—I just refuse to use the microwave for soup, it always gets boiling hot on the edges and stays ice cold in the middle, you know how that goes? And for dinner, well, I still try to make a proper meal, even if it takes me twice as long to stand there and chop the onions now because my arms feel so heavy. I'll do a nice meatloaf or a roast chicken. I always roast a chicken on Sundays, with the carrots and the little red potatoes all tucked around it in the pan to soak up the juices. 

So, yes, I'm still eating just about the exact same amount I always have. My stomach still rumbles right around noon, regular as a clock. I haven't noticed any difference at all in my appetite, really.

At first, I honestly just thought I was worn out from moving all her boxes and rearranging the house. We had to move the whole living room around just to fit her favorite recliner, and I'm not as young as I used to be. But the heaviness, it never went away, it just got deeper and deeper. \n\nAnd then, maybe a few weeks after she moved in, that's when those nighttime thoughts started happening. So yes, four whole months of this. Four months of going to sleep just hoping I wouldn't have to do it all over again the next day. It’s a long time to feel like that, isn't it? I kept waiting to just bounce back like I used to, thinking maybe once we got into a routine with her it would lift, but the days just keep blurring together and that dark cloud just stays right there.\n\nDoctor: Do you still find pleasure in activities that you used to enjoy before these feelings started?\n\nPatient: Well, doctor, that's... that's a sad thing to admit, really. Because if you asked anyone who knows me, they'd tell you I used to be quite the busy bee. My days were just full of things I loved doing. Like my painting... I used to look forward to my watercolors so much. I have this little setup right by the kitchen window—the light hits just perfectly there in the late afternoons, you see, right around four o'clock. I'd paint little birds, mostly, or whatever flowers were blooming out front in the beds. I just loved mixing the colors on this little plastic palette I got at the craft store... but lately, I just... I just leave my things sitting there. A group of us would go down to the community center for line dancing. We'd dance to those old country songs, and I even bought these special shoes with suede on the bottoms so you can slide real nice on the wood floor without scuffing it up. But now... I can't muster up a single ounce of joy for the music anymore, let alone the dancing. \n\nEven just walking with the ladies... I used to do that every Thursday, rain or shine, unless it was pouring, of course. We’d do a whole big loop around the park, catching up on all the neighborhood news, seeing whose grandkids were doing what, looking at the gardens. They still call me, bless them, they leave voicemails asking if I'm coming out with them, but I just let the phone ring. I tell myself I'll go, I really do, but then the time comes and... I just don't care about the walk, or the chatting, or any of it. She'll call out asking for a fresh glass of water, or she'll need help finding the television remote—she's always losing that little black remote down the side of the recliner cushions, you know, the one we had to move the whole room for—and I just feel this awful, ugly spike of irritation. \n\nAnd then, almost immediately, the guilt just crashes right down on me. I start thinking... I start thinking about what kind of a person I must be to feel that way. I tell myself I'm a bad woman. A truly bad, wicked woman for feeling annoyed at an elderly lady who just needs a little help and can't do for herself anymore. I feel like I'm bringing shame on my whole family for not being more grateful. I mean, I should be counting my blessings! I should be grateful we have a nice home and a spare room to put her in, but instead, I'm just sitting there at the kitchen table feeling resentful. It’s shameful, it really is. I just sit there and think about how worthless I am for not having a better heart about it all, and how I'm failing everyone by being so ungrateful. It just loops in my head, over and over, how bad I am for feeling annoyed...\n\nDoctor: Have you noticed any significant change in your weight over the past four months?\n\nPatient: Well, my weight... you know, I haven't really stepped on the scale in a while. Grab my cart, go straight to the produce, pick out the firmest tomatoes, and be done with it. My husband and I, we sit down right at 7:00 PM on the dot for Wheel of Fortune. We've been watching it for, oh, it must be thirty years now. Vanna always has the most beautiful gowns, doesn't she? And as for reading, well, I don't read big thick novels so much, mostly because my eyes get a little tired with these bifocals if the print is too small, but I still read my Reader's Digest from cover to cover. My sister gets me a subscription every year for my birthday, she never forgets. They have those wonderful little stories, you know, the 'Drama in Real Life' section? I read one just yesterday afternoon about a man who got stuck in a terrible snowstorm in his pickup truck for three whole days up in the Dakotas somewhere. I read the entire article in one sitting while I was resting my legs on the sofa. I didn't lose my place or find myself having to reread paragraphs or anything like that. So, no, my mind is still sharp as a tack when it comes to paying attention to my shows and my magazines, even if my body is just dragging behind.

Slow motion... well, it's funny you put it exactly that way, because that is exactly what my husband, Arthur, has been saying to me lately. He says I move like everything takes extra effort now, like I'm walking through molasses or something. And I suppose he's right, though I don't always notice it myself until he points it out. And I realized I had just been standing there... looking at them. For I don't know how long. I knew what I wanted, I knew I needed to reach out and put three of them in one of those little plastic bags on the roll, but I just... I couldn't seem to make my arm do it right away. 

It's like there's this delay between my brain telling my body to move and my body actually doing it. Even getting up from my recliner in the evening—it's a La-Z-Boy, the kind with the handle on the side, upholstered in this lovely sage green chenille—it takes me three or four tries to rock myself up, and then I just stand there for a minute before I take a step. I'm definitely not fidgety or restless, I can tell you that for sure. If anything, I'm just so terribly slow. It just takes everything out of me to get moving.

We were in the kitchen, and I was trying to get the good china down from the top shelf of the hutch—the set we got for our 25th anniversary, the one with the little gold rim—and he came in and told me that I move like everything takes extra effort now. Like I'm walking through molasses or something. He said I look so heavy when I walk, like just lifting my feet is a chore. \n\nAnd, you know, I didn't want to admit it to him right then, because I don't want him worrying, but he's right. Grab my cart, go straight to the produce, pick out the firmest tomatoes, and be done with it. It's like my brain knows what to do, but my body just takes so, so long to catch up. I just stand there for the longest time, staring, before I can finally get my arm to move and put a simple bag of carrots in the basket. It’s just so much harder to get anything done.\n\nDoctor: Do you feel like you have less energy than you used to?\n\nPatient: Energy... oh, my goodness, yes. It's just... I really don't know where it all went. Like I was telling you just a minute ago about my sleep, I spend a full night in bed, right? I get my rest, the whole night through, but when I wake up, my body just feels completely worn out. It just doesn't make any sense to me. I used to be up with the sun, ready to tackle the day, get the whole house in order before nine o'clock. \n\nBut now... well, just making that breakfast I told you about, the oatmeal for my aunt, it takes so much out of me. I find myself having to lean against the kitchen counter while the milk heats up because I just don't have the strength to stand there straight. And the laundry! Oh, heavens, the laundry. I have this old wicker basket, the one with the little floral cloth liner that ties at the corners—my daughter bought it for me at a craft fair years ago, such a pretty thing—and just carrying that basket from the bedroom down the hall to the washing machine... it feels like I've run a marathon. It just takes more out of me than it ever should. I actually have to sit down on the edge of the bed and catch my breath before I can even think about pouring the detergent or sorting the whites from the colors. I just don't have the pep I used to have, no matter how much I sleep.\n\nDoctor: Have you noticed any change in your appetite over the past four months?\n\nPatient: Appetite... well, no, I wouldn't say my appetite has changed much at all. I still eat my regular meals, just like always. It's funny you ask, though, because with how completely exhausted I feel, you'd think I just wouldn't have the stomach for it, but I still get hungry right on schedule. \n\nLike for breakfast... well, after I make that oatmeal for my aunt, I usually fix myself a slice of toast. She makes it from scratch every summer, boils the glass jars and seals them with the wax and everything. I'll heat it up on the stove—I just refuse to use the microwave for soup, it always gets boiling hot on the edges and stays ice cold in the middle, you know how that goes? And for dinner, well, I still try to make a proper meal, even if it takes me twice as long to stand there and chop the onions now because my arms feel so heavy. I'll do a nice meatloaf or a roast chicken. I always roast a chicken on Sundays, with the carrots and the little red potatoes all tucked around it in the pan to soak up the juices. \n\nSo, yes, I'm still eating just about the exact same amount I always have. My stomach still rumbles right around noon, regular as a clock. It pops up perfect every single time. And I'll put a little butter on it, and maybe some of the strawberry preserves my neighbor, Mrs. Gable, brings over. She makes it from scratch every summer, boils the glass jars and seals them with the wax and everything. She's such a sweet lady, always checking in on me. \n\nAnd then for lunch, it's usually just a half a sandwich or a little bowl of soup. Campbell's tomato, mostly, especially when it's damp out. I'll heat it up on the stove—I just refuse to use the microwave for soup, it always gets boiling hot on the edges and stays ice cold in the middle, you know how that goes? And for dinner, well, I still try to make a proper meal, even if it takes me twice as long to stand there and chop the onions now because my arms feel so heavy. I'll do a nice meatloaf or a roast chicken. I always roast a chicken on Sundays, with the carrots and the little red potatoes all tucked around it in the pan to soak up the juices. \n\nSo, yes, I'm still eating just about the exact same amount I always have. My stomach still rumbles right around noon, regular as a clock. No, I really haven't had any trouble with my concentration. I still watch my programs every evening just fine. My husband and I, we sit down right at 7:00 PM on the dot for Wheel of Fortune. We've been watching it for, oh, it must be thirty years now. Vanna always has the most beautiful gowns, doesn't she? I always tell my husband I'd love to know who her designer is, not that a woman my age has anywhere to wear a sequined floor-length dress! But I can follow the puzzles without any trouble at all.
